taxonomy.intro: Every signal on the site is read by a fixed, documented rule applied to the latest numbers — never a human judgement call. Here is exactly how each reading becomes the badge you see. There are four kinds of signal:
taxonomy.severity: Severity — most signals. A reading maps to one of four badges: ok, watch, elevated, or alert. The thresholds below are the real numbers the code uses; the marker on each lens page shows where the latest reading falls.
taxonomy.info: Descriptive — tracked for context, not scored. A higher or lower reading isn't itself better or worse, so there's no badge — just the number and its direction.
taxonomy.momentum: Momentum — a few market signals show which way a price is moving (up / down / flat) rather than a good-or-bad verdict.
taxonomy.neutral: Neutral scoreboards — two lenses (the asset-class scoreboard and crypto market structure) summarise how things are moving without aggregating to a good-or-bad verdict.

recession-watch::yield-curve.title: Yield Curve · 10-Year minus 2-Year
recession-watch::yield-curve.why: Not a static level — the curve scores by state. An inversion (below zero) is a classic recession warning that preceded every U.S. recession since the 1970s; a recent un-inversion warrants vigilance, because recessions historically begin after the curve climbs back above zero; a positive curve with no recent inversion is the all-clear.

recession-watch::sahm-rule.title: Sahm Rule Recession Indicator
recession-watch::sahm-rule.why: The Sahm rule trips at 0.50 — historically consistent with a recession already underway. 0.35–0.50 is the warning band as it climbs toward the trigger.

recession-watch::jobless-claims.title: Initial Jobless Claims · weekly
recession-watch::jobless-claims.why: Weekly initial jobless claims. Below ~250k, employers aren't shedding workers; 250–300k is a creeping rise; above 300k points to accelerating layoffs.

recession-watch::unemployment.title: Unemployment Rate
recession-watch::unemployment.why: Scored on the rise above the trailing-12-month low, not the raw level (the Sahm-style signal): a climb of 0.5 points or more off the recent low has preceded past downturns.

axis.label: the rise above the trailing-12-month low

cost-of-money::fed-funds.title: Federal Funds Rate
cost-of-money::fed-funds.why: The Fed's policy rate. At or above 4% is a restrictive stance worth flagging; the read also notes the ~12-month direction.

cost-of-money::treasury-10y.title: 10-Year Treasury Yield
cost-of-money::treasury-10y.why: Scored by level: above the watch line a Treasury yield is pricier than the post-2010 norm for borrowers; above the elevated line it's broadly restrictive. There is no 'alert' here — an expensive rate is a drag, not a crisis the way a default spike is.

cost-of-money::treasury-2y.title: 2-Year Treasury Yield
cost-of-money::treasury-2y.why: Scored by level: above the watch line a Treasury yield is pricier than the post-2010 norm for borrowers; above the elevated line it's broadly restrictive. There is no 'alert' here — an expensive rate is a drag, not a crisis the way a default spike is.

cost-of-money::rate-expectations.title: Rate Expectations · 2-Year minus Fed Funds
cost-of-money::rate-expectations.note: Whether markets expect cuts or hikes isn't itself good or bad — it's the bond market's forecast, shown for context.

job-market::unemployment.title: Unemployment Rate
job-market::unemployment.why: Scored on the rise above the trailing-12-month low, not the raw level (the Sahm-style signal): a climb of 0.5 points or more off the recent low has preceded past downturns.

axis.label: the rise above the trailing-12-month low

job-market::payrolls.title: Nonfarm Payrolls · monthly change
job-market::payrolls.why: Monthly jobs added. Outright job losses are an alert; under ~75k and ~150k are slowing-but-positive paces; above that is a healthy clip.

job-market::job-openings.title: Job Openings (JOLTS)
job-market::job-openings.why: Job openings (JOLTS), in millions. Below ~7.5M flags cooling labor demand.

job-market::wage-growth.title: Wage Growth · year-over-year
job-market::wage-growth.why: In the job-market frame, strong pay is healthy and stalling pay signals a softening labor market, so this warns on the LOW side: under 2% a year is stalled. (The inflation angle lives in Cost of Living's real wages.)

job-market::participation.title: Labor-Force Participation Rate
job-market::participation.note: This level drifts with demographics — the job-market verdict is carried by unemployment, payrolls, and job openings.

cost-of-living::cpi.title: Inflation · CPI (year-over-year)
cost-of-living::cpi.why: A year-over-year inflation rate (CPI, core, or PCE) against the Fed's 2% goal: near 2% is ok, 2.5–4% is still above target, 4%+ is hot.

cost-of-living::core-cpi.title: Core CPI (year-over-year)
cost-of-living::core-cpi.why: A year-over-year inflation rate (CPI, core, or PCE) against the Fed's 2% goal: near 2% is ok, 2.5–4% is still above target, 4%+ is hot.

cost-of-living::pce.title: PCE Inflation (year-over-year)
cost-of-living::pce.why: A year-over-year inflation rate (CPI, core, or PCE) against the Fed's 2% goal: near 2% is ok, 2.5–4% is still above target, 4%+ is hot.

cost-of-living::real-wages.title: Real Wage Growth (year-over-year)
cost-of-living::real-wages.why: Inflation-adjusted pay. Below zero means paychecks aren't keeping up with prices (watch); positive is ok.

fiscal-health::debt-gdp.title: Federal Debt · % of GDP
fiscal-health::debt-gdp.why: Federal debt versus the size of the economy. It crossed 100% around 2013; the bands mark high (90%), larger-than-the-economy (110%), and uncharted (130%).

fiscal-health::deficit-12m.title: Federal Deficit · trailing 12 months
fiscal-health::deficit-12m.why: The trailing-12-month deficit in trillions. The bands rise from a sizable structural deficit through crisis-era scale — the COVID peak was about $3T.

fiscal-health::interest-cost.title: Federal Interest Cost · annual rate
fiscal-health::interest-cost.note: The dollar interest bill climbs with the economy; the scored read is interest as a share of revenue, alongside debt-to-GDP and the deficit.

fiscal-health::interest-burden.title: Interest Cost · share of federal revenue
fiscal-health::interest-burden.why: Federal interest as a share of TOTAL receipts — the conventional ~20% figure. A record-high read prints 'elevated'; 'alert' is reserved for a genuinely unprecedented level above ~22%.

fiscal-health::receipts.title: Federal Receipts · year-over-year
fiscal-health::receipts.why: Scored on the year-over-year change where FALLING is the stress signal — profits, new-business applications, capital-goods orders, sales. Growth is ok; the bands mark progressively deeper contractions.

bank-asset-quality::noncurrent.title: Noncurrent Loan Rate · loans 90+ days past due
bank-asset-quality::noncurrent.why: Loans 90+ days past due as a share of all loans. Under 1% is low by historical standards; 1–2% is creeping; above 2% is elevated.

bank-asset-quality::charge-offs.title: Net Charge-Off Rate · annualized
bank-asset-quality::charge-offs.why: Loans written off as losses. Under ~0.6% is benign; the bands mark where losses become a meaningful drag on earnings.

bank-profitability::net-margin.title: Net Interest Margin · annualized
bank-profitability::net-margin.why: Net interest margin. Below ~2.5% is a compressed spread that squeezes bank earnings.

bank-profitability::roa.title: Return on Assets · annualized
bank-profitability::roa.why: Return on assets. 1%+ is solid bank profitability; 0.5–1% is subdued; below 0.5% is weak.

bank-capital-solvency::risk-based-capita.title: Total Risk-Based Capital Ratio
bank-capital-solvency::risk-based-capita.why: The regulators' headline solvency gauge: 10%+ is 'well-capitalized', 8–10% adequate, below 8% under the minimum.

bank-capital-solvency::equity-assets.title: Equity-to-Assets
bank-capital-solvency::equity-assets.why: Equity-to-assets. Banks historically run ~9–11%; below 9% is on the lighter side, below 7.5% is a thin cushion.

bank-concentrations-funding::uninsured.title: Uninsured-Deposit Share
bank-concentrations-funding::uninsured.why: Deposits above the $250k FDIC cap — the money most likely to flee in a panic, as at Silicon Valley Bank. Above ~40% is flight-prone.

bank-concentrations-funding::loans-depos.title: Loans-to-Deposits
bank-concentrations-funding::loans-depos.why: Loans as a share of deposits. Above ~90% means the system's funding is stretched.

bank-concentrations-funding::cre-concent.title: CRE Concentration · % of capital
bank-concentrations-funding::cre-concent.why: Commercial real estate as a share of bank capital. Above ~300% is the interagency supervisory concentration flag; ~200% is a notable build.

market-risk-sentiment::vix.title: Volatility · VIX
market-risk-sentiment::vix.why: The equity 'fear gauge'. Below 20 is calm; 20–30 is nervous; 30+ is fearful.

market-risk-sentiment::hy-spread.title: High-Yield Credit Spread
market-risk-sentiment::hy-spread.why: The extra yield investors demand over Treasuries. Tight spreads signal calm credit; the bands mark where spreads have historically started to price real default risk (the high-yield band sits wider than investment-grade because junk spreads are structurally larger).

market-risk-sentiment::ig-spread.title: Investment-Grade Credit Spread
market-risk-sentiment::ig-spread.why: The extra yield investors demand over Treasuries. Tight spreads signal calm credit; the bands mark where spreads have historically started to price real default risk (the high-yield band sits wider than investment-grade because junk spreads are structurally larger).

market-risk-sentiment::nfci.title: Financial Conditions · NFCI
market-risk-sentiment::nfci.why: The Chicago Fed NFCI, where zero is average. Positive means tighter (more stressed) than normal; 0.5+ is tight.

market-scoreboard::sp500.note: Part of a neutral scoreboard — it shows which way the price is moving, not whether that's good or bad.

market-liquidity::m2-growth.title: M2 Money Supply · year-over-year
market-liquidity::m2-growth.why: Money-supply growth, two-sided: double-digit growth is historically inflationary (2020–21), while an outright contraction is rare and signals a monetary squeeze (2022–23). The calm band is roughly -1% to 7%.

market-liquidity::fed-balance-sheet.title: Fed Balance Sheet · total assets
market-liquidity::fed-balance-sheet.note: A descriptive level of the monetary plumbing — this lens's verdict is carried by M2 money-supply growth.

consumer-spending::retail-sales.title: Retail Sales · year-over-year
consumer-spending::retail-sales.why: Scored on the year-over-year change, two-sided: both an overheating boom and a sharp contraction raise severity, because each is its own kind of instability. The quiet middle band is ok.

consumer-spending::real-spending.title: Real Consumer Spending · year-over-year
consumer-spending::real-spending.why: Scored on the year-over-year change, two-sided: both an overheating boom and a sharp contraction raise severity, because each is its own kind of instability. The quiet middle band is ok.

consumer-spending::auto-sales.title: Vehicle Sales · annual rate
consumer-spending::auto-sales.why: Light-vehicle sales (annual-rate millions) — the big-ticket purchase households cut first. ~15M+ is healthy; the 2009 and 2020 troughs near 9M anchor the alert band.

consumer-credit::card-delinquency.title: Credit-Card Delinquency Rate
consumer-credit::card-delinquency.why: Delinquency-rate levels, calibrated against history — bank credit-card delinquency peaked near 6.8% in 2009. Low and steady is ok; climbing toward past-crisis levels escalates.

consumer-credit::consumer-delinquency.title: Consumer-Loan Delinquency Rate
consumer-credit::consumer-delinquency.why: Delinquency-rate levels, calibrated against history — bank credit-card delinquency peaked near 6.8% in 2009. Low and steady is ok; climbing toward past-crisis levels escalates.

consumer-credit::revolving-credit.title: Card Balances · year-over-year
consumer-credit::revolving-credit.why: Credit-card balance growth. Growing faster than incomes (8%+) means households are leaning on cards; shrinking balances mean paying down.

consumer-credit::debt-service.title: Household Debt Service · % of income
consumer-credit::debt-service.why: Household debt payments as a share of income. Above ~10.5% is above the comfortable range; the 2007 danger level of ~13% anchors the alert band.

consumer-income-savings::saving-rate.title: Personal Saving Rate
consumer-income-savings::saving-rate.why: The personal saving rate — the household shock absorber. The historical norm is 5–8%; below 5% is thin, below 3% is almost no cushion.

consumer-income-savings::real-income.title: Real Disposable Income · year-over-year
consumer-income-savings::real-income.why: Inflation-adjusted disposable income, the root of most consumer stress. Below zero is a warning; a 2%+ annual drop erodes purchasing power fast.

consumer-income-savings::net-worth.title: Household Net Worth · year-over-year
consumer-income-savings::net-worth.why: Scored on the year-over-year change where FALLING is the stress signal — profits, new-business applications, capital-goods orders, sales. Growth is ok; the bands mark progressively deeper contractions.

consumer-sentiment::sentiment.title: Consumer Sentiment (U. Michigan)
consumer-sentiment::sentiment.why: U. Michigan consumer sentiment, long-run range roughly 50–110. 85+ is fine; the bands step down through recession-grade gloom; the 2022 record low was about 50.

consumer-sentiment::inflation-expectatio.title: Inflation Expectations · 1-year ahead
consumer-sentiment::inflation-expectatio.why: One-year-ahead household inflation expectations, which the Fed watches for de-anchoring. Above ~3% is a touch high; 5.5%+ suggests expectations coming unmoored.

energy-oil-fuels::gasoline.title: Retail Gasoline · Regular
energy-oil-fuels::gasoline.why: Scored on the trailing-12-month change, because what strains a household is how fast a cost is rising, not its dollar level. The bands reflect how volatile each fuel or power price normally is; a falling cost reads as relief (ok).

energy-oil-fuels::diesel.title: Retail Diesel · On-Highway

energy-oil-fuels::crude-production.note: A physical supply-and-demand reading, not a household cost — this lens's verdict comes from the price indicators.

energy-commodities::food-index.why: A cost already expressed as a year-over-year rate. Same logic as the fuel costs: faster annual increases mean more household strain; flat or falling is ok.

housing-home-prices::case-shiller.why: Scored on the year-over-year change, two-sided: both an overheating boom and a sharp contraction raise severity, because each is its own kind of instability. The quiet middle band is ok.

housing-home-prices::existing-home-sales.title: Existing-Home Sales · annual rate
housing-home-prices::existing-home-sales.why: Two-sided on the trailing-12-month change: a market running too hot (a bubble) and one freezing (a bust) are both unhealthy, so both raise severity. The calm middle is a balanced market.

housing-home-prices::median-price.title: Median Sales Price of Houses Sold
housing-home-prices::median-price.why: Two-sided on the trailing-12-month change: a market running too hot (a bubble) and one freezing (a bust) are both unhealthy, so both raise severity. The calm middle is a balanced market.

housing-affordability::affordability-ind.title: Housing Affordability Index (NAR)
housing-affordability::affordability-ind.why: The NAR affordability index, where 100 means the median family just barely affords the median home. Higher is better, so the bands are inverted: 130+ is comfortable, below 95 is out of reach.

housing-affordability::debt-service.title: Mortgage Debt Service · % of income
housing-affordability::debt-service.why: Mortgage payments as a share of income, calibrated to its own history: median ~6.1%, the 2007 peak ~7.2%, the early-1980s extreme ~8.9%.

housing-affordability::delinquency.title: Mortgage Delinquency Rate · banks
housing-affordability::delinquency.why: Single-family mortgages past due at banks. Under 2% is healthy; the bands climb toward the 2009 crisis peak of about 11%.

housing-affordability::mortgage-rate.title: 30-Year Fixed Mortgage Rate
housing-affordability::mortgage-rate.why: 30-year mortgage-rate levels. Below ~5.5% is moderate by recent standards; the bands step up through where affordability gets stretched (6.5%) and where most buyers are frozen out (7.5%).

housing-supply-construction::months-supp.title: Months of New-Home Supply
housing-supply-construction::months-supp.why: Months of new-home supply, two-sided: 4–6 months is balanced, under 3 is a tight market that props up prices, and 8+ is a glut that pressures builders.

housing-supply-construction::active-list.title: Active Listings (Realtor.com) · millions
housing-supply-construction::active-list.note: Months' supply, which adjusts for the sales pace, carries this lens's supply verdict; this is the raw count for context.

housing-supply-construction::housing-sta.title: Housing Starts · thousands, annual rate
housing-supply-construction::housing-sta.why: Two-sided on the trailing-12-month change: a market running too hot (a bubble) and one freezing (a bust) are both unhealthy, so both raise severity. The calm middle is a balanced market.

housing-supply-construction::building-pe.title: Building Permits · thousands, annual rate
housing-supply-construction::building-pe.why: Two-sided on the trailing-12-month change: a market running too hot (a bubble) and one freezing (a bust) are both unhealthy, so both raise severity. The calm middle is a balanced market.

housing-rent-shelter::rent-cpi.why: A cost already expressed as a year-over-year rate. Same logic as the fuel costs: faster annual increases mean more household strain; flat or falling is ok.

housing-rent-shelter::owners-equivalent-.title: Owners' Equivalent Rent · year-over-year
housing-rent-shelter::owners-equivalent-.why: A cost already expressed as a year-over-year rate. Same logic as the fuel costs: faster annual increases mean more household strain; flat or falling is ok.

housing-rent-shelter::rental-vacancy.title: Rental Vacancy Rate
housing-rent-shelter::rental-vacancy.why: Rental vacancy, two-sided: 6–8% is a healthy balance, low vacancy gives landlords pricing power (rent pressure), and high vacancy hands it back to renters.

housing-rent-shelter::homeownership.title: Homeownership Rate
housing-rent-shelter::homeownership.note: A descriptive level shown for context — neither a high nor a low reading is simply good or bad.

global-dollar-currencies::dollar-yoy.title: Broad Dollar Index · year-over-year
global-dollar-currencies::dollar-yoy.why: The broad dollar's year-over-year move, scored two-sided on magnitude: a surging dollar squeezes the world's dollar borrowers and a sliding one imports inflation, so both raise severity. Under ~5% is normal drift.

global-growth::world-growth.why: Annual world real-GDP growth, scored against its long-run trend of about 3.5%. Below roughly 2% is what economists call a global recession; the bands step down from trend toward that line.

global-trade-supply::gscpi.title: Global Supply Chain Pressure Index
global-trade-supply::gscpi.why: The NY Fed supply-chain pressure index, in standard deviations from normal. Negative is looser than normal (ok); the bands climb toward extreme disruption (the COVID peak was about 4.5σ).

global-trade-supply::trade-balance.title: U.S. Trade Deficit · goods & services
global-trade-supply::trade-balance.note: The U.S. has run a trade deficit every year since 1976 — the level isn't good or bad on its own; what matters is the trend shown here.

global-uncertainty::us-epu.title: U.S. Economic Policy Uncertainty
global-uncertainty::us-epu.why: The Baker/Bloom/Davis policy-uncertainty index, whose long-run norm is about 100, so the bands mark multiples of that norm. The global index is capped at 'watch' because it publishes about six months late — a stale read shouldn't drive a live alarm.

business-formation::hp-share.title: High-Propensity Share of Applications
business-formation::hp-share.note: A descriptive level shown for context — neither a high nor a low reading is simply good or bad.

business-investment::core-capex.title: Core Capital-Goods Orders · year-over-year
business-investment::core-capex.why: Scored on the year-over-year change where FALLING is the stress signal — profits, new-business applications, capital-goods orders, sales. Growth is ok; the bands mark progressively deeper contractions.

business-investment::real-sales.title: Real Business Sales · year-over-year
business-investment::real-sales.why: Scored on the year-over-year change where FALLING is the stress signal — profits, new-business applications, capital-goods orders, sales. Growth is ok; the bands mark progressively deeper contractions.

business-investment::inventories-sales.title: Inventories-to-Sales Ratio
business-investment::inventories-sales.why: Inventories measured in months of sales. Above ~1.50 is an overhang that typically forces production cuts; 2008 peaked near 1.48, COVID near 1.74.

business-credit::baa-spread.title: Baa Corporate Spread · over 10-Year Treasury
business-credit::baa-spread.why: Moody's Baa corporate yield over the 10-year Treasury — the price of ordinary corporate credit risk. Calm is under 2 points; 2008 peaked near 6, which anchors the alert band.

business-credit::lending-standards.title: Lending Standards · net % of banks tightening
business-credit::lending-standards.why: The net share of banks tightening business-loan standards (the Fed's loan-officer survey). Easing is ok; sustained tightening above ~20% is a classic late-cycle signal; 2008 hit about 84%.

business-credit::delinquency.title: Business-Loan Delinquency Rate
business-credit::delinquency.why: Business loans past due at banks. Under 1.5% is healthy; the bands climb toward the 2009 peak of about 4.4%.

business-credit::ci-loan-growth.title: C&I Loan Growth · year-over-year
business-credit::ci-loan-growth.why: Scored on the year-over-year change, two-sided: both an overheating boom and a sharp contraction raise severity, because each is its own kind of instability. The quiet middle band is ok.
